# Clone integration harness — cross-engine, cross-generation

Runs the clone (`Meadow-Service-Sync-*`) against **real source APIs** and a
**real MySQL clone target** in Docker, and asserts what lands in the clone after
each step of a create → update → delete → **un-delete** lifecycle.

The clone image is built from the **local working tree**, not from what npm
ships, so it tests uncommitted changes. The first check in every run verifies
that patch landed; if it didn't, nothing else in the run means anything.

```bash
./Run.sh          # both source generations
./Run.sh 4x       # current stack only
./Run.sh 2x       # legacy stack only
```

## What it stands up

| Service     | Stack                                                            | Store            |
|-------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------|
| `source-4x` | meadow-endpoints 4.x / orator 6 / fable 3 (retold-data-service)   | PostgreSQL, or MSSQL |
| `source-2x` | meadow-endpoints 2.1.1 / meadow 1.0.35 / orator 2.0.10 / restify 6.4.0 | MySQL 5.7   |
| `clone`     | meadow-integration from the working tree                         | → MySQL 5.7      |

Each leg clones into its own database (`clone4x`, `clone2x`) and resets its
source between runs, so the legs are independent and repeatable.

## Two constraints worth knowing

**SQL Server needs its CPUs pinned on hosts with a gapped CPU mask.** SQLPAL
aborts at startup (`GetEndOfLibOSVmRange(): Assertion IsLibOSVmmRangeEndValid()`)
when the online CPU list has holes — check with `lscpu | grep -i off-line`. The
`mssql` service pins `cpuset: 0-7`; override with `MSSQL_CPUSET` if that range
isn't fully online on your host. This is the same workaround the Lastrada local
MSSQL importer takes (`tools/integration/lastrada`, `--cpuset` option).

```bash
docker compose --profile mssql up -d mssql
SOURCE_ENGINE=mssql docker compose up -d --build source-4x
SOURCE_ENGINE=mssql docker compose run --rm clone node validate.js 4x
```

PostgreSQL is the default source engine so the 4.x leg runs with no pinning
needed; both engines are verified at 24/24.

**The 2.x leg is MySQL-backed.** meadow 1.0.x ships providers for MySQL and
ALASQL only — there is no MSSQL or PostgreSQL provider for that generation — so
a meadow-endpoints 2.x source has to be MySQL, which is also what the Headlight
API runs against in production.

## Source-generation differences the harness exercises

- **Exposing the deleted set.** Stock meadow-endpoints 2.1.1 honors
  `FBV~Deleted~EQ~1` on its own. Headlight's 2.x API does not (its controller
  qualifies column names before foxhound checks for an existing `Deleted`
  filter), so the clone appends `?includeDeleted=true`. The 2.x leg runs with
  that query string configured, which confirms it stays harmless where the
  filter already works.
- **Restoring a record.** 4.x has `GET /1.0/Book/Undelete/:IDRecord`. 2.x has no
  such route, and `PUT` cannot clear the flag either — its pre-update read is
  delete-tracked, so it answers `Record not found`. The 2.x leg therefore
  restores the record in the source store directly, which is the only option an
  operator has on that generation today.

## Why the un-delete assertions look the way they do

A restored record must come back as an **update to the row already there**. The
older code could not see its own soft-deleted row (the existence check was
delete-tracked), so it attempted an identity insert over it instead. What that
costs depends on the target engine:

The recovery hinges on `JSON.stringify(error)` containing "duplicate"/"unique",
which is a property of the driver, not of the clone:

| Clone target | Old code recovers? | Why |
|--------------|--------------------|-----|
| SQLite       | **No — record stays deleted** | node:sqlite exposes only `{code, errcode, errstr}`; `message` is non-enumerable |
| MySQL        | Yes                | `sqlMessage: "Duplicate entry…"` is enumerable |
| MSSQL        | Yes                | `originalError.info.message` carries "duplicate key" |
| PostgreSQL   | Yes, by luck       | nothing says "duplicate" — it matches only because `routine: "_bt_check_unique"` contains "unique" |

On every engine except SQLite the failed insert is recoverable, so the record
lands correctly anyway — just noisily, and only after meadow's collision
pre-flight has renamed the live row's GUID to `__mdsd_…` on the way through.

Because this harness clones into MySQL, asserting only on the end state would
pass either way. So it also asserts on **how** the record was reconciled — the
run fails if the sync log shows the duplicate-key recovery path. The
engine-specific data loss itself is covered by
`test/Meadow-Integration-CloneUndeleteSync_test.js`, which runs against SQLite.

## Checks per leg (24)

Harness integrity · initial sync fidelity (count, titles, identities, flags) ·
new records · edited records · source deletions · **un-delete: live again, GUID
preserved, values caught up, no duplicate row, no collision-rename, reconciled
as a plain update** · repeat-sync stability · delete/restore round trip ·
records deleted before they were ever cloned are still not backfilled.
